section.title: Final Greetings
section.sectionRationale: The letter closes as it opened, with grace and a circle of names. Fellow prisoners and fellow workers send greetings, and Paul ends with the same grace of the Lord Jesus that framed the whole appeal, now prayed over the church's spirit.
section.thesis: Paul signs off surrounded by a company of fellow prisoners and workers and leaves the church with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the grace that alone makes the whole appeal for Onesimus possible.
section.frameNote: One movement: greetings from Paul's companions, and a closing blessing of grace on the church's spirit.

units.label: Greetings and closing grace
units.note: a company of witnesses and a final blessing

verses.text: Epaphras, my {{synaichmalotos|fellow prisoner}} in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings,
as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my {{synergos|fellow workers}}.
The {{charis|grace}} of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your {{pneuma|spirit}}.

synaichmalotos.gloss: A fellow prisoner or fellow captive, literally one taken captive alongside another, drawn from the language of prisoners of war. Epaphras shares Paul's imprisonment for the gospel, showing that Paul is not alone even in chains; the family of Christ stands with him.

synergos.gloss: A fellow worker or co-laborer, the same word Paul used of Philemon in verse 1. He now names Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke as his fellow workers, drawing Philemon into a wider fellowship of gospel partners and quietly reminding him that he too shares this labor of love.

charis.gloss: Grace, undeserved favor and kindness. The letter ends where it began, with grace, verse 3. This final grace is the power behind the whole appeal: only grace received can make a master welcome a runaway slave as a beloved brother.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, the inner person, here the seat of one's life before God. Paul prays grace upon your spirit, using a plural you that widens the blessing to the whole gathered church, so that all who heard the letter are left resting in the grace of Christ.

basic.context: Paul ends the letter the way he began it, with grace and with a group of names. Epaphras, who is in prison with him, sends greetings, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, Paul's fellow workers. Then Paul closes with a blessing: may the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. The you here is plural, so the blessing reaches the whole church, not just Philemon.
basic.hermeneutics: Even the closing greetings do quiet work. By naming a circle of companions, Paul reminds Philemon that a whole gospel family is watching and standing with him, and that he belongs to something larger than his household. And by ending with grace, Paul leaves the deciding word not on duty but on the grace that makes obedience possible.
basic.originalLanguages: Epaphras is Paul's synaichmalotos, his fellow prisoner. Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke are his synergoi, fellow workers, the same word used of Philemon in verse 1. And the letter ends with charis, grace, upon your pneuma, your spirit, the plural you gathering the whole church into the blessing.
basic.typology: There is no formal type here, but the closing grace embodies the letter's theme. The grace that saves and reconciles, flowing from the Lord Jesus, is the same grace that must flow from Philemon to Onesimus, a small echo of the grace that flows from God to us and through us to others.
basic.christ: The last word is the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Everything the letter asks rests on Him: His grace saved Philemon, converted Onesimus, and alone can turn a master and a slave into brothers. Christ has the final word, as He has the first.
basic.god: God surrounds His servants with a family even in prison, and He leaves His people not with a burden but with grace. He is the God who gives what He commands, supplying by grace the very love and welcome He calls for.
basic.crossReferences: Colossians 4:10-14 lists the same companions, tying the two letters together. Galatians 6:18 ends with the same blessing of grace with your spirit. Second Timothy 4:10-11 later mentions Demas, Mark, and Luke again, with differing outcomes.
basic.oneStory: The letter ends on grace, and so does the Bible. The grace of the Lord Jesus is the thread from the first promise to the last page, the power that reconciles God to sinners and sinners to one another, and here it is prayed over a church learning to live out that reconciliation.

context.literary:
Verses 23 to 25 are the closing of a letter, and Paul's closings are never filler. Ancient letters usually ended with greetings and a short farewell, but Paul turns the form into theology, and here the ending does careful work against the opening. The letter began with two names in the sender's line, Paul and Timothy, and a crowd in the address: Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in the house, verses 1 and 2. It ends with five more names sending greetings. The little letter is bracketed by people, and in between lies a request that touches all of them.

Look at the pronouns. Almost everything from verse 4 to verse 21 is addressed to one person, 'you' singular, and Paul presses Philemon in the first person: 'I appeal,' 'I am sending him back,' 'I will repay it.' Then in verse 22 the 'you' turns plural, 'your prayers,' 'restored to you,' and it stays plural through the last line, 'with your spirit.' Greek has a plural pronoun that English hides. The letter that read like a private note is, in its closing lines, read aloud to the household church that was named in verse 2. Philemon cannot answer in private.

Verse 25 also closes a frame. The letter opened with 'Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,' verse 3, and it ends with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Everything in between, the thanksgiving, the appeal, the offer to repay, sits inside those two graces. The central request is not left hanging in the air; it is held between two blessings, as a gift is held in cupped hands.

Finally, notice the order of the names in verse 24. Mark is first and Luke last, and the list closes with 'my fellow workers,' a title that sends the reader back to verse 1, where Philemon himself is called by the same word.
context.historical:
The names in these verses are all people we can follow elsewhere, and that is what gives them weight. Mark is the John Mark whose mother's house was a place of prayer in Jerusalem, Acts 12:12. He left Paul and Barnabas at Perga and went home, Acts 13:13, and Paul later refused to take him again, so sharp a quarrel that Paul and Barnabas parted company, Acts 15:37-39. By the time of this letter the breach is healed. Paul counts Mark among his fellow workers, and in Colossians 4:10 he tells the church to welcome him if he comes. A man who once let Paul down is now standing in the greetings of a letter that asks a master to receive a man who let him down.

Aristarchus was a Macedonian from Thessalonica who was seized with Paul in the riot at Ephesus, Acts 19:29, travelled with him, Acts 20:4, and boarded the ship with him for Rome, Acts 27:2. Luke is the physician called beloved in Colossians 4:14. Epaphras was the man through whom the Colossians first heard the gospel, Colossians 1:7, and he, Colossians 4:12-13, was always wrestling in prayer for the churches of the Lycus valley, Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis. Philemon lived in Colossae, so Epaphras is a neighbour, not a stranger. Colossians 4:9 even says that Onesimus 'is one of you.'

The same list appears in Colossians 4:10-14, with a small swap. In Colossians it is Aristarchus who is the 'fellow prisoner' and Epaphras is called a servant of Christ; here Epaphras holds the prison title. Many take this to mean that the companions took turns sharing Paul's confinement, voluntarily sharing his captivity, while others simply came and went. The Colossians list adds Jesus called Justus, who does not appear here. These details show that both letters were composed and delivered at the same time, probably carried by Tychicus and Onesimus together, Colossians 4:7-9.

The place of imprisonment is debated, but Acts 28:30-31 gives the house arrest in Rome, where Paul 'welcoming all who came to visit him,' a setting in which friends could come, go and send greetings.
context.canonical:
Paul's closings are a small genre of their own, and reading them side by side teaches how deliberate they are. The blessing of this letter, 'The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit,' is almost word for word the ending of Galatians 6:18 and Philippians 4:23. Other letters expand it: 2 Corinthians 13:14 adds the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, so that the three persons are named in a benediction. Titus 3:15 and Hebrews 13:25 shorten it to 'Grace be with all of you.' Whatever else Paul says, he never closes a letter without it. For him grace is not a decoration on the end of an argument; it is the air the argument breathes.

The same names reappear in other letters and tell a longer story. In 2 Timothy 4:10-11 Paul, now near the end of his life, writes that Demas, 'in his love of this world, has deserted me,' and that 'only Luke is with me.' Of Mark he says, 'Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry.' The man once sent away is now wanted. Mark appears too as 'my son Mark' beside Peter in 1 Peter 5:13. Read together, the lists are an honest record: some stay, some leave, some are restored.

The concern about slaves and masters, which shaped the letter, finds its answer in the New Testament as a whole, Galatians 3:28 and Ephesians 6:5-9, and the quiet note of reconciliation in the last verses anticipates Colossians 3:11, where 'slave, or free' fall away because 'Christ is all and is in all.'

Revelation 22:21 closes the whole Bible with the same grace: 'The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints.' A short letter about one runaway ends the way the entire canon ends.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's aim in a closing is relational. He means to keep Philemon from feeling alone with his decision, and also from feeling alone with Paul's pressure. By naming companions who know Onesimus, who know Philemon, and who know the stakes, he turns a one to one request into a request made in the open among friends. He does not threaten; he lets love be seen.

He also means the church in the house to overhear. The plural in verse 25 is not a slip. Whatever Philemon decides will be shaped in the hearing of a community that Paul has already addressed, verse 2, and the blessing is spoken over all of them. Paul wants a whole congregation to learn what forgiveness between a master and a slave looks like, long before any rule has been written.

The last aim is the quietest. Paul ends by handing the matter to Christ. He has argued, appealed, offered to pay, and hinted that he expects more than he asks, verse 21. Now he stops. The final sentence does not instruct; it blesses, and in doing so it admits that what he is asking cannot be produced by pressure. Only the grace of the Lord Jesus can make a free and glad welcome.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything in these verses is description. Epaphras sends greetings; the five workers are named; Paul prays. None of it is a command, and it would be a mistake to turn the list of names into a rule that every letter must contain greetings, or that every Christian must be imprisoned, or that Demas is always a warning.

What the text does show is how Paul's ministry actually lived: never alone, always among people who cared about the churches and about each other. That is worth imitating as a pattern of life and not as a law. A believer who serves in isolation is working against the grain of the New Testament.

The closing blessing is a prayer and not a command, yet it carries a prescription of its own. Believers are meant to pray this grace over one another, and to expect it to be what carries even the hardest obedience. The grace that is prayed for here is the same grace that, in other letters, trains believers to live well, Titus 2:11-12. It is the only fuel for the costly welcome the letter has asked Philemon to give.

debates.question: Why does Paul list so many names in so short a letter?

views.label: To place public weight behind a private appeal
views.case: Naming Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke gives Philemon a sense of being watched with love by respected people. It also signals that these men are friends of Onesimus, so the welcome Paul asks for is one the whole circle would approve. The plural 'you' in verses 22 and 25 fits a letter meant to be heard by the church in Philemon's house, verse 2.

views.label: Simply the warm closing of a close company
views.case: Letters of the period carried greetings, and Paul's others do the same, Romans 16, Colossians 4, 2 Timothy 4. On this view the names are the ordinary courtesy of friends, and to read pressure into them would be to read too much.

debates.bearing: The two views do not compete. Paul's courtesy is real, and it also works for the gospel, since a genuine fellowship is what makes the appeal bearable and not merely binding.

debates.question: Where was Paul when he wrote this letter?

views.label: Rome
views.case: The tradition of the church and Acts 28:30-31 place Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years, receiving visitors. His hope in verse 22 to be restored to Philemon fits a prisoner expecting release. Luke and Aristarchus, who sailed to Rome with him in Acts 27:2, are both in the greetings.

views.label: Ephesus
views.case: Some propose Ephesus because it lies roughly a hundred miles from Colossae, a runaway slave could reach it more easily, and Paul's hope to visit Philemon would be a short journey. The imprisonment there is not described in Acts, but Paul speaks of serious hardships in Asia, 2 Corinthians 1:8-9.

views.label: Caesarea
views.case: Others point to the two years Paul was held in Caesarea, Acts 24:27, as another possible site, though it lies furthest from Colossae.

debates.bearing: The placing does not change what the closing teaches. Wherever Paul was, he was in chains, surrounded by friends, and still sending greetings.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's vocabulary in these three verses is chosen with care, and several of his words repay a closer look than the basic study gave them.

Verse 23 calls Epaphras synaichmalotos, from aichme, a spear, and a verb meaning to capture, so literally a captive of the spear, a prisoner of war. Paul uses it of Andronicus and Junia in Romans 16:7 and of Aristarchus in Colossians 4:10, and nowhere else do we find it. A military term is turned to a spiritual one. Elsewhere Paul calls Philemon's friend Archippus a 'fellow soldier,' verse 2, and Epaphroditus the same, Philippians 2:25. The imprisoned apostle sees himself, and those who share his confinement, as soldiers taken in a war that Christ has already won.

Paul writes 'in Christ Jesus,' en Christo Iesou, with the phrase that governs the whole letter. Epaphras is a prisoner in Christ, not of Rome. The phrase echoes Paul's opening, 'a prisoner of Christ Jesus,' verse 1, and shows who he thinks holds the keys.

Verse 24 uses synergoi, a compound of syn, with, and ergon, work, so a fellow worker, or literally one who works alongside. Paul calls Prisca and Aquila by it, Romans 16:3, and Timothy, Romans 16:21, and Epaphroditus, Philippians 2:25. In verse 1 Philemon is also his synergos. The shared title means that when Paul closes by listing five workers, he is quietly saying that Philemon belongs to the same company, and that the company expects him to act like it.

Verse 25 is the most important grammatically. The phrase is charis, grace, followed by meta, 'with,' and the genitive 'your spirit.' There is no verb in the Greek. English supplies 'be,' the sense of a wish, but the original simply declares: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, with your spirit. The effect is closer to a statement of presence than to a hope. The word hymon, 'your,' is plural, as is the word for 'you' in verse 22, but the noun 'spirit' is singular, pneuma, as if the whole church shares one spirit. This is the idiom of Galatians 6:18 and Philippians 4:23.

Finally, the title kyrios, Lord, joined to Iesous Christos, the full name, Lord Jesus Christ, is the same threefold form that opened the letter in verse 3. To call Jesus kyrios is to give Him the Greek word the Septuagint uses for the covenant name of God, a point Paul makes in Philippians 2:11. The letter that deals with a human lord and a human slave ends by naming the one Lord over both.

typology.type: The company of prisoners and fellow workers
typology.fulfillment: Paul is not alone in his chains because Christ's people have always shared one another's burdens. The picture of captives who stay near to prisoners foreshadows the call of Hebrews 13:3, 'Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them,' and Christ's own words that visiting a prisoner is visiting Him, Matthew 25:36. The correspondence is real, but the type is imperfect: human companions come and go, and Demas will leave, while Christ is the companion of whom God says, 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you,' Hebrews 13:5.

typology.type: Mark, the failed servant welcomed back
typology.fulfillment: Mark's history, Acts 13:13, then Acts 15:37-39, then 2 Timothy 4:11, is a small enacted picture of forgiveness and restoration among believers. It is not a formal type, but it shows the gospel working before Philemon's eyes: a man who deserted his post is called useful and welcomed among fellow workers. It points to the larger restoration of Peter after his denial, John 21:15-17, and ultimately to the Father's welcome of the returning son, Luke 15:20-24. The limit is that Mark's welcome came from a human friend; our welcome is earned by Christ alone.

typology.type: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ as the closing benediction
typology.fulfillment: The benediction of Numbers 6:24-26, 'The LORD bless you and keep you,' is the pattern behind every Christian blessing. In Christ it is fulfilled and deepened, since 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,' John 1:17, and from His fullness 'we have all received grace upon grace,' John 1:16. Paul says Christ became poor so that we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9, which is the pattern of what Philemon is asked to do for Onesimus. The type falls short only in that Aaron's blessing was spoken by a priest over the people; the grace of Christ is given by the Lord Himself.

study.christ:
The letter ends with a title, 'the Lord Jesus Christ,' and the title is the whole argument in small. Christ is Lord, which means that Philemon, who owns a household, answers to one who owns him. Christ is Jesus, a name for the Saviour who took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7. And Christ is the anointed King who rules what Philemon rules. Paul does not need to command because he has already appealed to the one whose authority is above both of them.

Notice too the way Paul connects Christ with grace in a unique way. He does not write 'the grace of God' but 'the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ,' a phrase he repeats at the close of letter after letter. Grace has a face and a name. It is not an abstract kindness but the character of a particular person who, 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. That is the pattern the letter has been holding up to Philemon: a rich man giving up his rights for the sake of a poor man.

The whole story of Onesimus is a small copy of the gospel. Onesimus owes a debt, and Paul says, 'I will repay it,' verse 19, and then, 'receive him as you would receive me,' verse 17. Paul steps between the offender and the offended and offers his own account in exchange, which is what Christ did for sinners when He took on Himself the debt that was not His. The letter never says this directly, and a reader should be careful not to turn Paul into a Christ figure. But it is plain that the shape of his request is the shape of the cross.

Finally, Christ is the one who makes a new relationship between people possible. Paul speaks of Onesimus as 'a beloved brother,' verse 16, and elsewhere of the old walls coming down, Ephesians 2:14-16, Galatians 3:28. When the closing blessing asks that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with their spirit, it asks that the fellowship Christ created would be the final fact in a household where, by the standards of the world, a master and a slave could never be brothers.
study.god:
This closing says several things about God, mostly by what it takes for granted.

God is a God who gathers. The list of names is the visible fruit of a God who calls people from different places, Macedonia, Colossae, Jerusalem, and makes them a company. Mark was a Jerusalem man, Aristarchus a Macedonian, Luke likely a Gentile, Epaphras a local from the Lycus valley. They are scarcely a natural team. The God of this passage creates a family, and does so especially in prison, where such bonds could easily be broken.

God is also the one who sustains in hardship. Paul never presents his chains as a defeat. He writes from prison and expects to be released through prayer, verse 22. There is no bitterness in the greetings. The prisoner is not a victim but a servant under the sovereign care of God, who uses even confinement to bring a runaway slave to faith, verse 10.

God is the giver of grace as the very condition of obedience. Paul has asked Philemon to do something costly. Instead of ending with a threat, he ends by praying for what would make obedience possible. The letter does not say 'do this in your own strength,' but 'may the grace of the Lord Jesus be with your spirit.' That is a doctrine in miniature: God supplies what He demands, as Paul says elsewhere, 'by the grace of God I am what I am,' 1 Corinthians 15:10. This is consistent with the way Scripture speaks of God from Exodus onward, as the one who rescues first and gives the law afterwards.

The trinitarian shape also bears noting. The letter opens with 'God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,' verse 3, and ends with the Lord Jesus Christ. In 2 Corinthians 13:14 the same blessing grows to include the Spirit. Paul does not argue the doctrine in Philemon, but he prays in a way that would be meaningless unless the Lord Jesus were truly divine, for no mere human could be asked to be present with the spirits of a whole congregation.

For worship, this should shape how we end our gatherings. A benediction is not a polite way of saying goodbye. It is a declaration that God has not left, and the church goes out with the Lord Jesus Himself.

crossReferences.note: The parallel list of greetings, sent at the same time. Aristarchus is the fellow prisoner there, and Epaphras 'always wrestling in prayer' for the Colossians. The overlap confirms the two letters travelled together, and shows Epaphras's care for the very town where Philemon lived.

Epaphras is the one from whom the Colossians learned the gospel, 'a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf.' When he sends greetings to Philemon, he is greeting someone he served, which makes his presence among Paul's companions more tender.

Years later Demas has gone, 'in his love of this world,' and Mark is wanted as 'useful to me in the ministry.' The two verses show that the companionship of Philemon 24 was not permanent: some leave, and some who failed once are restored.

The sharp quarrel over Mark that split Paul and Barnabas. Set beside Philemon 24 it makes Mark's inclusion more striking: the man Paul once refused to take is now a fellow worker, which is exactly the kind of reconciliation Paul hopes for between Philemon and Onesimus.

The closing is almost identical, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ with your spirit. Paul's pairing of grace and spirit at the end of a letter that argues for freedom shows he ends consistently on the same note.
Another letter written from prison ends with the same words, 'with your spirit.' The repetition shows grace as Paul's habitual last word, and in a prison letter it becomes especially pointed.

A fuller form of the same blessing, adding the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. It shows the Trinitarian background to the shorter closing in Philemon, where only the Lord Jesus is named.
Paul's other use of the word for fellow prisoner, of Andronicus and Junia, who were 'in Christ before I was.' It shows the term was a badge of honour among believers who had suffered alongside him.

The church that meets in Philemon's house is named at the start, and the plural 'your spirit' at the end sends the blessing back to the same group. The letter that began with a household closes by blessing the same household.
The Bible's last sentence is the same blessing, 'The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints.' The closing of a letter about one runaway matches the closing of the whole canon.

study.oneStory:
Philemon is a short letter about a runaway, and it sits in the long story of a world that has lost its way and a God who comes after it. This closing shows where that story has reached. In Genesis 3 humanity ran from God and hid; a master and a slave, a free man and a captive, are some of the sad results of that first flight. Everything in Scripture since has been God moving toward the fugitives, and the people who belong to Him moving toward each other.

The Old Testament had hints of this. Israel itself was freed from slavery, Exodus 20:2, and told to treat the slave and the stranger with the memory of that rescue in mind, Deuteronomy 15:15. The law gave the slave limited protection, Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 23:15-16, but the harder work of changing hearts was reserved for a later day. The prophets spoke of a day when God would put His Spirit within His people, Ezekiel 36:26-27.

In Philemon that day has begun. A slave who ran from his master has been found by Christ in a prison cell, and the master is asked to receive him not as property but as a brother. The company named in verses 23 and 24 is a sample of the new people, drawn from Macedonia, Jerusalem and Colossae, and the grace of verse 25 is the means by which the new humanity is held together. The deep division of master and slave is, in Christ, not abolished by decree but made powerless by love, Galatians 3:28.

The story is not finished. Demas will drift and Mark will be restored; the church will continue to struggle. But the ending is secure. In Revelation 7:9 a great multitude from every nation, tribe and language stands before the throne, and in Revelation 22:21 the Bible closes with the same grace that closes this letter. Between those two scenes, Philemon is a window into how it is lived out in a single household: grace meeting a debt, a family replacing a hierarchy, and a company of friends who hold one another up until the day they will see the Lord Jesus face to face.

sermon.title: Refresh My Heart
sermon.why: The closing message of Begg's series A Study in Philemon covers Philemon 1:17-25, including these final greetings, and draws the letter to a close on the grace of the Lord Jesus and the fellowship of the gospel. A faithful, orthodox handling of this movement.

quiz.q: Who does Paul describe as his fellow prisoner in these closing verses?

options.text: Epaphras, his fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus.
options.note: Epaphras, the evangelist of Colossae, shares Paul's imprisonment, verse 23.

options.text: Aristarchus, one of his named companions.
options.note: In Colossians 4:10 Aristarchus is called Paul's fellow prisoner, but in Philemon that title is given to Epaphras.
Luke is named among the fellow workers, not as the fellow prisoner here.
Timothy is named in the opening greeting, not here as fellow prisoner.

quiz.q: How does Paul end the letter?

options.text: With a blessing: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
options.note: The letter closes on grace, framing the whole appeal, verse 25.

options.text: With warm greetings from his companions and a final blessing.
options.note: The greetings do come just before, but the letter's final words are the blessing of grace.

options.text: With a stern final warning to obey.
options.note: Paul closes with grace, not with a threat.
Paul ends with the grace of Christ, not a financial appeal.

quiz.q: Why does Paul name a circle of coworkers in such a personal letter?

options.text: To surround the appeal with loving witnesses and remind Philemon he belongs to a wider gospel family.
options.note: The named companions add warm accountability and fellowship to the private request.

options.text: To pass along the genuine greetings of real friends in the faith.
options.note: These are real friends sending real greetings, and their inclusion also lends warm accountability to the appeal.

options.text: To fill space at the end of the letter.
options.note: The greetings are meaningful, not filler; they connect Philemon to a watching family.

options.text: To boast about how many friends he has.
options.note: The point is genuine fellowship and witness, not boasting.

quiz.q: What is the significance of ending the letter with grace?

options.text: Grace is the power behind the whole appeal; only grace received can make Philemon welcome Onesimus as a brother.
options.note: The letter opens and closes on grace, resting the outcome on Christ rather than duty.

options.text: It is only a standard sign-off with no real meaning.
options.note: It is Paul's customary close, but here it carries the whole weight of the appeal.

options.text: It means Philemon is free to ignore the request.
options.note: Grace enables the obedience Paul expects; it does not cancel it.

options.text: It shows Paul had run out of things to say.
options.note: The closing grace is a deliberate and fitting frame for the letter.

questions: Even in prison Paul was surrounded by a family of fellow workers. Who are the companions God has given you for the long road of following Christ, and are you keeping those bonds?
Paul left Philemon not with pressure but with grace. When you face a hard obedience, do you draw on grace, or try to grit it out on duty alone?
The same grace that saved Philemon was the grace he had to pass on to Onesimus. Where is God asking you to extend to someone the grace you yourself have received?
Demas is a fellow worker here but later deserted Paul. What helps you keep going faithfully rather than drifting away over time?
The letter begins and ends with grace. How would your relationships change if grace framed both the start and the finish of your dealings with others?

translationNotes.note: Fellow prisoner renders synaichmalotos, literally a fellow captive of war; Epaphras shared Paul's imprisonment for the gospel.
The same companions, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, are named in Colossians 4:10-14, sent from the same imprisonment.
Your spirit uses a plural you, widening the closing blessing to the whole gathered church. Some manuscripts, BYZ and TR, add Amen, as the BSB footnote notes.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Philemon 1:23-25. BYZ and TR add Amen at the end of verse 25, per the BSB footnote; the BSB main text omits it and is followed here.
